posts.title: Taster evening on 2 February: what happens in the hour and a half
posts.excerpt: Our next taster evening is on Tuesday 2 February 2027, from 18:30 to 20:00 at 3 Weaver’s Yard.
posts.content:
Come at half past six and Yara Lindqvist, our admissions officer, will meet you at the door. At 18:45 you learn your first signs with Noor Haddad or Pieter Laine, with no voices in the room.

At 19:30 there is time to ask about the courses, the timetable and the fees. The room is step-free and has a hearing loop, and interpreters are present. The evening is free and you do not need to sign.

The next evenings are Tuesday 2 February, 2 March and 6 April 2027, 18:30–20:00.

posts.title: What we talk about at the Saturday table
posts.excerpt: Every Saturday afternoon at Yubi College, eighteen adult learners and their tutors close their notebooks to examine the morning’s interpreting scenes honestly and without grades.
posts.content:
By 14:00 on Saturday, the role-play rooms at 3 Weaver’s Yard have gone quiet. For three hours, eighteen second-year Diploma students have worked in pairs across mock consultation rooms, court benches, and classroom desks. They have interpreted for role-players playing doctors explaining medication dosages, magistrates managing bail hearings, and teachers discussing reading progress with parents. Now, everyone gathers around the long pale-wood table in the main room. The morning’s clipboards are set aside and notebooks stay closed.

Helena Varga, principal of the college, sits at one end of the table, while Elias Brandt, head of interpreting practice, and Deaf language tutors Noor Haddad and Pieter Laine sit among the students. Tomasz, who works night shifts as a staff nurse at Esterhaven General Hospital, sits across from Adaeze, an office manager at Harrow Field Primary. There are no grades handed out, no scores marked on paper, and no reprimands. The purpose of the afternoon table is simple: to examine the exact moment where spoken words met sign language, and to discover what the person on the receiving end actually understood.

Today, the discussion begins with a mock outpatient scenario at Esterhaven General Hospital. Tomasz had interpreted for a Deaf patient played by Pieter, who was consulting a role-player doctor about a complex cardiac prescription. In the heat of the interaction, Tomasz softened the physician’s blunt warning about side effects, hoping to spare the patient unnecessary distress. Noor does not criticize his intention, but asks Tomasz to replay the exchange entirely in sign language. Standing before the group, Tomasz signs the physician’s true instruction again, realizing that omitting the severity deprived the patient of the information needed to make an informed choice.

Across the table, Adaeze reflects on what she observed from the observer’s chair. In the Thursday lab booths, students learn the technical craft of voice and sign delivery, working in pairs where one interprets and the other logs timing and omissions. But Saturday setting mornings introduce the unpredictable friction of human emotion and institutional pressure. Adaeze notes how physical positioning in the room altered the sightlines between doctor and patient, creating unnecessary confusion. Ruth Abiodun, healthcare interpreting tutor, nods and explains how hospital furniture arrangements can dictate the success of an entire clinical consultation.

This weekly rhythm—two weekday evenings after work and a full Saturday of immersive simulation and debriefing—forms the core of the Yubi College method. Founded in 1996 by Johanna Reiss and Tobias Mendel, the college was built specifically for working adults who cannot abandon their livelihoods to retrain. By dissecting mistakes in a supportive circle the very day they occur, students develop the emotional stamina and professional ethics required for high-stakes environments. While the Diploma prepares you to apply to the interpreter register where you live, the true standard of practice is forged right here at the table, where the hands that carry the words learn to carry truth without compromise.

posts.title: Three habits from outpatients
posts.excerpt: Ruth Abiodun on three habits she asks every healthcare student to practise before their first placement.
posts.content:
Ruth Abiodun leads the healthcare certificate. Before a student's first outpatients placement she asks for three habits. Introduce yourself to both people before anyone speaks. Ask for a pause before a number or a dose. Say aloud when you need something repeated.

None of these is about vocabulary. They are the small, plain moves that keep a consultation accurate, and they are practised on Saturday mornings in the mock clinic until they are automatic.
